claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B showing reduced protein levels of the mutant, with inference about degradation.

claims.claim: GRA16WT-HA is exported into the host cell where it accumulates in the nucleus.
claims.source: GRA16WT-HA was observed within the host cell nucleus, as previously reported (Bougdour et al., 2013), as well as at the PV and within parasites (Figure 1C-i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence assay data shown in Figure 1C-i and is consistent with previous published work.

claims.claim: GRA16AAAAE-HA export to the host cell is severely impaired compared to GRA16WT-HA.
claims.source: In contrast, GRA16AAAAE-HA was observed either within parasites, in small punctate structures reminiscent of the Golgi or in the PV space between parasites (Figure 1C-ii). In a minority of cells, a small amount of exported GRA16AAAAE-HA could be observed within the host nuclei (Figure 1C-ii, panel 2); however, there was a large and clear defect in export in the mutant line.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1C-ii showing altered localization of the mutant protein.

claims.claim: The PEXEL-like motif is required for correct proteolytic processing of GRA16 and efficient export to the host cell.
claims.source: Taken together, this demonstrates that the PEXEL-like motif is required for correct proteolytic processing of GRA16 and efficient export to the host cell.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on GRA16 processing and localization.

claims.claim: The PEXEL-like motif in Toxoplasma is termed the Toxoplasma export element (TEXEL).
claims.source: We therefore termed this motif the Toxoplasma export element (TEXEL).
claims.evidence: The claim is a nomenclature decision based on the functional characterization of the motif.

claims.claim: ASP5 (TGME49_242720) is the top BLAST hit when searching ToxoDB using P. falciparum PMV as a query.
claims.source: We searched ToxoDB (http://toxodb.org) using P. falciparum PMV (PfPMV) as a query and the top Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) hit was aspartyl protease 5 (ASP5, TGME49_242720), consistent with previous phylogenetic analysis of this group of proteases in Apicomplexa (Shea et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST search results and is consistent with previous phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: ASP5 and P. falciparum PMV share approximately 33% similarity and 14% identity across the full-length alignment.
claims.source: An alignment of the two proteins revealed that they share approximately 33% similarity and 14% identity across the full-length alignment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: ASP5 and PMV share several key features including an N-terminal signal peptide, a core aspartyl protease domain with DTG and DSG catalytic dyad residues, a plant-like nepenthesin fold, and a C-terminal transmembrane domain.
claims.source: The proteins shared several key features, including an N-terminal SP, a core aspartyl protease domain (with DTG and DSG residues defining the catalytic dyad), a plant-like nepenthesin fold, as well as a C-terminal transmembrane domain (Hodder et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and comparison with known structural features, citing previous work.

claims.claim: ASP5 contains a significantly longer signal peptide and C-terminal tail sequence than PMV.
claims.source: While ASP5 contains a significantly longer SP and C-terminal tail sequence than PfPMV, it lacks the helix-turn-helix motif found in PMV from all Plasmodium spp. that is hypothesized to interact with other ER proteins (Hodder et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison between ASP5 and PMV.

claims.claim: ASP5 lacks the helix-turn-helix motif found in PMV from all Plasmodium species.
claims.source: While ASP5 contains a significantly longer SP and C-terminal tail sequence than PfPMV, it lacks the helix-turn-helix motif found in PMV from all Plasmodium spp. that is hypothesized to interact with other ER proteins (Hodder et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison and structural analysis.

claims.claim: ASP5WT-HA3 is present as two major species of approximately 90 and 55 kDa.
claims.source: Immunoblot analysis with anti-HA antibodies revealed ASP5WT-HA3 is present as two major species of approximately 90 and 55 kDa (Figure 2A), consistent with a signal peptidase-cleaved species and possibly an activated form, respectively (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: ASP5MUT-HA3 (D431A, D682A) is observed predominantly as the ~90 kDa form, suggesting that ASP5 may auto-activate to produce the ~55 kDa species.
claims.source: A mutant form of ASP5, where the conserved aspartic acid catalytic residues were mutated to alanine (ASP5D431A, D682A-HA3; herein referred to as ASP5MUT-HA3), was observed predominantly as the ~90 kDa form, suggesting that ASP5 may auto-activate to produce the ~55 kDa species (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data comparing wild-type and mutant ASP5, with inference about auto-activation.

claims.claim: ASP5WT-HA3 localizes to the Golgi and co-localizes with the Golgi marker GalNAc-YFP.
claims.source: Using immunofluorescence microscopy with anti-HA antibodies, we observed ASP5WT-HA3 in apical puncta that co-localized with GalNAc-YFP, a known Golgi marker (Nishi et al., 2008) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating co-localization with a known Golgi marker.

claims.claim: ASP5MUT-HA3 localizes to discrete puncta adjacent to the nucleus, representative of the Golgi.
claims.source: ASP5MUT-HA3 also localized to discrete puncta adjacent to the nucleus, representative of the Golgi (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Immunoprecipitated ASP5WT-HA3 cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL peptide (DABCYL-R-VSRRLAEEP-E-EDANS).
claims.source: Immunoprecipitated ASP5WT-HA3, but not ASP5MUT-HA3, cleaves GRA16 TEXEL (DABCYL-R-VSRRLAEEP-E-EDANS) but not the RRL>AAA peptide.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorogenic peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Immunoprecipitated ASP5MUT-HA3 does not cleave the GRA16 TEXEL peptide.
claims.source: Immunoprecipitated ASP5WT-HA3, but not ASP5MUT-HA3, cleaves GRA16 TEXEL (DABCYL-R-VSRRLAEEP-E-EDANS) but not the RRL>AAA peptide.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorogenic peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: ASP5WT-HA3 does not cleave the GRA16 TEXEL peptide when the RRL motif is mutated to AAA.
claims.source: Immunoprecipitated ASP5WT-HA3, but not ASP5MUT-HA3, cleaves GRA16 TEXEL (DABCYL-R-VSRRLAEEP-E-EDANS) but not the RRL>AAA peptide.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorogenic peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: ASP5 cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL peptide after the leucine residue (RxL↓xE/Q/D).
claims.source: Peptides incubated in buffer alone remained intact in contrast to peptides incubated with ASP5WT-HA3, which resulted in the generation of a product corresponding to processing within the TEXEL after leucine (DABCYL-R-VSRRL↓). This processing event after the leucine residue, hereafter referred to as the P1 position, is the identical site of processing of the PEXEL by PMV in both P. falciparum and P. vivax (Boddey et al., 2009; 2010; Russo et al., 2010; Sleebs et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 2D identifying the cleavage site.

claims.claim: ASP5WT-HA3 efficiently cleaves the GRA16 peptide with Km 47.8 ± 18.4 μM.
claims.source: ASP5WT-HA3 efficiently cleaved the GRA16 peptide with Km 47.8 ± 18.4 μM (mean ± SD) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: ASP5WT-HA3 activity is optimal at pH 5.5.
claims.source: ASP5WT-HA3 activity was optimal at pH 5.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), in contrast to pH 6.4 for PMV (Boddey et al., 2010; Russo et al., 2010), consistent with the Golgi being a more acidic environment than the ER (Wu et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pH optimization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: The optimal pH for ASP5 activity (pH 5.5) is consistent with the Golgi being a more acidic environment than the ER.
claims.source: ASP5WT-HA3 activity was optimal at pH 5.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), in contrast to pH 6.4 for PMV (Boddey et al., 2010; Russo et al., 2010), consistent with the Golgi being a more acidic environment than the ER (Wu et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of pH optima and known pH differences between organelles.

claims.claim: WEHI-586 (RRLStatine) inhibits ASP5WT-HA3 with IC50 of 63 ± 15 nM.
claims.source: Incubation of ASP5WT-HA3 with WEHI-586 blocked cleavage of the GRA16 peptide with IC50 of 63 ± 15 nM (mean ± standard error of the mean) (Figure 2F), demonstrating the potent affinity of the TEXEL sequence for ASP5.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response inhibition data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: ASP5 is a Golgi-resident protease that cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL motif after the leucine residue.
claims.source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that ASP5 is a Golgi-resident protease that cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL motif after the leucine residue and can be potently inhibited by a TEXEL-mimetic small molecule.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on localization, cleavage site, and inhibition data.

claims.claim: PfPMV-HA cleaves peptides containing the wild-type KAHRP PEXEL but not P3 (R>K) or P1 (L>I) point mutations.
claims.source: PfPMV-HA behaved as expected (Boddey et al., 2010; 2013), cleaving peptides containing the WT KAHRP PEXEL but not P3 (R>K) or P1 (L>I) point mutations (Figure 3A-i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3A-i and is consistent with previous publications.

claims.claim: PfPMV-HA cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL peptide with notably higher efficiency than it cleaves the KAHRP PEXEL peptide.
claims.source: This Plasmodium enzyme also cleaved the peptide containing the WT GRA16 TEXEL, with notably higher efficiency than it cleaved the peptide KAHRP; however, it did not cleave GRA16 peptides containing TEXEL mutations at P3 (R>A) or P1 (L>A), as expected based on the known specificity of this protease (Figure 3A-i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparative peptide cleavage data shown in Figure 3A-i.

claims.claim: ASP5 cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL peptide but does not cleave peptides containing mutations at P3 (R>A) or P1 (L>A).
claims.source: Similarly, ASP5 cleaved the GRA16 TEXEL peptide but did not cleave peptides containing mutations of the TEXEL, P3 (R>A) or P1 (L>A), demonstrating that the P3 and P1 positions of the substrate (i.e. arginine and leucine, respectively) are important for ASP5 activity, as is the case for PMV (Figure 3A-ii) (Boddey et al., 2010; Russo et al., 2010; Sleebs et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3A-ii.

claims.claim: ASP5 does not cleave KAHRP PEXEL peptides above background levels.
claims.source: In contrast to PMV, ASP5 did not cleave KAHRP peptides above background levels (Figure 3A-ii).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3A-ii.

claims.claim: Replacement of the P2 residue in the KAHRP PEXEL (threonine) with arginine (P2 T>R) results in a 3-fold increase in cleavage by ASP5.
claims.source: Replacement of the P2 residue in the KAHRP PEXEL (threonine) with the corresponding residue in GRA16 (arginine) (i.e. P2 T>R) resulted in a 3-fold increase in cleavage, demonstrating the importance of the P2 position for ASP5 activity, although cleavage of this peptide was still well below that seen for the native GRA16 TEXEL peptide (Figure 3A-ii).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3A-ii.

claims.claim: ASP5 and PMV both cleave peptides containing RxL sequences but do not share identical substrate specificity.
claims.source: This demonstrates that while ASP5 and PMV both cleave peptides containing RxL sequences, they do not share identical substrate specificity.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from comparative peptide cleavage data.

claims.claim: ASP5 does not well tolerate conservative and non-conservative changes at the P1, P2 or P3 positions.
claims.source: This demonstrated that ASP5 does not well tolerate conservative and non-conservative changes at the P1, P2 or P3 positions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by point mutation analysis of the GRA16 TEXEL substrate.

claims.claim: ASP5 can cleave RKL at approximately 35-40% of wild-type activity.
claims.source: It appeared that ASP5 could cleave RKL at ~35–40% of WT, yet the physiological relevance of this is not known (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Mutation of the GRA16 TEXEL P2' residue E>A results in enhanced processing by ASP5.
claims.source: Interestingly, mutation of the GRA16 TEXEL P2' residue E>A resulted in enhanced processing, illustrating that this position in ASP5 substrates may not be essential for activity, similar to PMV, but can alter cleavage efficiency (Boddey et al., 2009; 2010; Sleebs et al., 2014a; 2014b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data and comparison with PMV.

claims.claim: ASP5 cleaves the wild-type GRA19 TEXEL peptide (RRLSD) efficiently.
claims.source: The WT GRA19 TEXEL peptide was processed efficiently and this was inhibited when the TEXEL was mutated from RRL to AAA (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: ASP5 does not process the RELLD sequence in GRA21.
claims.source: In contrast, the RELLD sequence in GRA21, and the corresponding AAALD mutant, were not processed by ASP5 (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: ASP5 likely processes GRA21 at the RRLAE position, which is the same sequence as the TEXEL in GRA16.
claims.source: Since the RRLAE in the N-terminus of GRA21 is the same sequence as the TEXEL in GRA16, it is highly likely that ASP5 processes GRA21 at this position.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on sequence similarity and known ASP5 specificity.

claims.claim: ASP5 has a relatively strict requirement for arginine at P3 and P2, and leucine at P1 of its substrates.
claims.source: Taken together, this work demonstrates that ASP5 has relatively strict requirement for arginine at P3 and P2, and leucine at P1 of its substrates (Figure 3D), and that residues at P1' and P2' are dispensable for processing but can influence the efficiency of cleavage by this enzyme.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on peptide cleavage data and is illustrated in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Residues at P1' and P2' are dispensable for ASP5 processing but can influence the efficiency of cleavage.
claims.source: Taken together, this work demonstrates that ASP5 has relatively strict requirement for arginine at P3 and P2, and leucine at P1 of its substrates (Figure 3D), and that residues at P1' and P2' are dispensable for processing but can influence the efficiency of cleavage by this enzyme.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on peptide cleavage data.

claims.claim: The guanidyl side-chain of arginine at P3 of the GRA16 TEXEL forms interactions with the side-chains of E506 and Q549 in ASP5.
claims.source: The model shows that the guanidyl side-chain of arginine at P3 (the first position in the TEXEL sequence) forms interactions with the side-chains of E506 and Q549 in a manner completely analogous to that observed in the structure of PMV in complex with the statine inhibitor, WEHI-842 (Hodder et al., 2015) (Figure 3E-i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 3E-i.

claims.claim: The leucine at P1 of the TEXEL is surrounded by hydrophobic residues I429, Y503, F546 and I554 of ASP5.
claims.source: Furthermore, the leucine at P1 of the TEXEL is surrounded by hydrophobic residues I429, Y503, F546 and I554 of ASP5; the isoleucine at position 554 in ASP5 is a valine in PMV, while the other residues, I, Y, F are identical between ASP5 and PMV (Figure 3E-i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 3E-i.

claims.claim: The AutoDock potential predicts that ASP5 binds the GRA16 peptide (SRRLAEE) 5 kJ/mol more tightly than an SRTLAEE mutant form.
claims.source: This was supported using our model, as the AutoDock potential predicted that ASP5 binds the GRA16 peptide (SRRLAEE) 5 kJ/mol more tightly than an SRTLAEE mutant form of GRA16 (Figure 3E-ii).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3E-ii.

claims.claim: The guanidine side-chain of arginine at P2 of native GRA16 forms hydrogen bonds with the side-chain hydroxyl of S505 and the backbone carbonyl of A776 in ASP5.
claims.source: The guanidine side-chain of arginine at P2 of native GRA16 forms hydrogen bonds with the side-chain hydroxyl of S505 and the backbone carbonyl of A776 (Figure 3E-i), whereas the mutated GRA16 substrate containing threonine at P2 forms only a single hydrogen bond with the side-chain hydroxyl of S505 (Figure 3E-ii).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 3E-i.

claims.claim: The differences in hydrogen bonding between arginine and threonine at P2 account for approximately 50% of the total difference in calculated binding affinity between the two substrates.
claims.source: Taken together, these differences in binding interactions accounts for ~50% of the total difference in the calculated binding affinity between the two substrates, providing a clear structural explanation for the substrate specificity (i.e. RRL) observed for ASP5.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of binding energies from the structural model.

claims.claim: Mutation of leucine at P1 of the GRA16 TEXEL to valine reduces the calculated binding energy by 6 kJ/mol.
claims.source: Mutation of leucine at P1 of the GRA16 TEXEL to valine reduces the calculated binding energy by 6 kJ/mol, which is in line with our observations that mutations at this position significantly reduce ASP5 activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling and is consistent with experimental data.

claims.claim: Mutation of alanine at P1' to valine is predicted to slightly increase the binding energy by less than 1 kJ/mol.
claims.source: Mutation of alanine at P1' (position 4 of the GRA16 TEXEL, RRLAE) to valine is predicted to slightly increase the binding energy, but by less than 1 kJ/mol.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling.

claims.claim: Mutation of glutamine at P2' to alanine causes an 11 kJ/mol reduction in calculated binding affinity in the model.
claims.source: Interestingly, mutation of glutamine at P2' (position 5 of the GRA16 TEXEL) to alanine causes an 11 kJ/mol reduction in calculated binding affinity in the model, in contrast to the increase in ASP5 activity observed in vitro (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling, though it contrasts with experimental data.

claims.claim: The ASP5 gene was successfully disrupted using a double homologous recombination strategy combined with an ASP5-targeted CRISPR approach.
claims.source: Utilizing a double homologous recombination strategy combined with an ASP5-targeted CRISPR approach, we were able to successfully disrupt the ASP5 gene, where the 3' flank underwent homologous recombination, while apparent lack of NotI cleavage and the presence of a Cas9-induced cut site resulted in the whole plasmid integrating non-homologously at that site, meaning that a green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression cassette also integrated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PCR and sequencing data confirming the gene disruption.

claims.claim: Δasp5 parasites produce smaller plaques than wild-type parasites in a 7-day plaque assay.
claims.source: To determine overall qualitative changes in asexual growth rate, WT and Δasp5 tachyzoites were grown for 7 days in a plaque assay (Figure 4A-i) and we observed that the plaques of the Δasp5 parasites were smaller than those generated by WT parasites, demonstrating that Δasp5 parasites have a clear growth disadvantage under simple in vitro growth conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by plaque assay data shown in Figure 4A-i.

claims.claim: The growth defect of Δasp5 parasites is restored following complementation with a stably-integrated copy of ASP5.
claims.source: This defect was restored following complementation with a stably-integrated copy of ASP5 (Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3) driven from the tubulin promoter (Figure 4A-ii.)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by plaque assay data shown in Figure 4A-ii.

claims.claim: Δasp5CRISPR tachyzoites have no major difference in intracellular replication compared to wild-type or Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 parasites at 16 hours post infection.
claims.source: From this analysis, it is clear that Δasp5CRISPR tachyzoites have no major difference in intracellular replication to either WT or Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 parasites.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by replication assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The smaller plaque size of Δasp5CRISPR tachyzoites is not due to retardation in replication.
claims.source: This suggests that smaller plaque size of Δasp5CRISPR tachyzoites, compared to WT and Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 parasites, is not due to retardation in replication.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the replication assay data.

claims.claim: In Δasp5 parasites, GRA16-HA migrates as a larger protein that has not been processed correctly.
claims.source: Western blot analysis of GRA16-HA in otherwise WT parasites yielded the same three bands as seen in Figure 1B, consistent with cleavage within the TEXEL motif, whereas in the Δasp5 parasites, GRA16-HA migrated as a larger protein that had not been processed correctly, mirroring the GRA16AAAAE-HA profile (Figure 4C, Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: GRA16-HA is no longer exported into the host cell during infection with Δasp5 parasites.
claims.source: While GRA16-HA produced by WT parasites was observed in the host nucleus as expected, this effector was no longer exported into the host cell during infection with Δasp5 parasites and instead appeared to localize to an internal structure reminiscent of the Golgi and in the PV space (Figure 4D), similar to the GRA16AAAAE-HA mutant (Figure 1C-ii).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Processing by ASP5 is essential for correct trafficking of GRA16 from the parasite into the infected host cell.
claims.source: This confirms that processing by ASP5 is essential for correct trafficking of GRA16 from the parasite into the infected host cell.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the processing and localization data of GRA16 in wild-type and Δasp5 parasites.

claims.claim: Toxoplasma tachyzoites actively induce expression of host c-Myc following infection.
claims.source: It has recently been shown that Toxoplasma tachyzoites, but not the related Neospora species, actively induce expression of host c-Myc following infection (Franco et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous work.

claims.claim: Activation of c-Myc by Toxoplasma was not induced in response to parasite invasion or injection of rhoptry proteins.
claims.source: This activation of c-Myc was not induced in response to parasite invasion or injection of rhoptry proteins (Franco et al., 2014), suggesting that one or more dense granule proteins may be responsible.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous work and inference about dense granule proteins.

claims.claim: HFFs infected with Δasp5 parasites express approximately 6.4-fold less c-Myc than those infected with wild-type parasites.
claims.source: Quantification by IFA showed that HFFs infected with parasites lacking ASP5 expressed approximately 6.4-fold less c-Myc than those infected with WT parasites (normalized ratio of c-Myc to 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole [DAPI]) (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: ASP5 is required for Toxoplasma to induce c-Myc in infected cells.
claims.source: To confirm this, c-Myc induction was measured by immunoblot of whole cell protein fractions. While c-Myc expression was induced in host cells infected with WT parasites, the signal was dramatically reduced in HFFs infected with the same number of Δasp5 parasites (Figure 5C), confirming that ASP5 is required for Toxoplasma to induce c-Myc in infected cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The up-regulation of c-Myc induced by tachyzoites is controlled by one or more ASP5-dependent proteins.
claims.source: Together, this work suggests that the up-regulation of c-Myc induced by tachyzoites is controlled by one or more ASP5-dependent proteins.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the requirement of ASP5 for c-Myc induction.

claims.claim: MYR1 is processed approximately two-thirds along its sequence, revealing a C-terminal fragment that migrates at ~32 kDa and an N-terminal fragment that migrates at ~80 kDa.
claims.source: Very recently, a novel dense granule protein was identified by the Boothroyd laboratory that localizes to the PV and is processed approximately two-thirds along its sequence, revealing a C-terminal fragment that migrates at ~32 kDa and an N-terminal fragment that migrates at ~80 kDa (Figure 6A) (Franco et al., in press).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data and citation of work in press.

claims.claim: MYR1 contains a TEXEL-like RRLSE sequence approximately 230 residues from the C-terminus.
claims.source: Analysis of this protein, MYR1 (TGGT1_254470), revealed a TEXEL-like RRLSE sequence approximately 230 residues from the C-terminus, the approximate position where cleavage is predicted to occur (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and schematic representation in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: In Δasp5 mutants, MYR1 is no longer processed and instead migrates at ~105 kDa.
claims.source: In the Δasp5 mutants, MYR1 is no longer processed and instead migrates at ~105 kDa (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: ASP5 is required for cleavage of MYR1.
claims.source: This strongly suggests that ASP5 is required for cleavage of MYR1.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the loss of MYR1 processing in Δasp5 parasites.

claims.claim: ASP5WT-HA3 efficiently cleaves the MYR1 TEXEL peptide (RRLSE), similar to the GRA16 RRLAE control.
claims.source: We found that ASP5WT-HA3 efficiently cleaved the MYR1 TEXEL peptide, similar to the GRA16 RRLAE control, whereas mutations of the conserved RRL residues abolished this activity (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The P1' residue (serine in MYR1 vs. alanine in GRA16) is not as constrained as the P1-3 positions for ASP5 activity.
claims.source: This demonstrates that MYR1 contains a TEXEL sequence that can be processed by ASP5. It also suggests that the P1' residue, which naturally differs between GRA16 (alanine) and MYR1 (serine), is not as constrained as the P1-3 positions, and confirms that the P2' residue is not essential for processing, since the MYR1 TEXEL P2' (E>A) mutant peptide was efficiently processed.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison of MYR1 and GRA16 TEXEL cleavage.

claims.claim: Mutation of the MYR1 TEXEL from RRLSE to ARLSE or ARASA prevents cleavage in vivo.
claims.source: While ectopic expression of the C-terminally tagged MYR1WT-HA resulted in detection of the expected ~32 kDa species, mutation of either RRLSE>ARLSE or RRLSE>ARASA prevented cleavage, leaving only the unprocessed species migrating at ~105 kDa (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The RRLSE sequence of MYR1 is necessary for processing in parasites.
claims.source: Thus, this sequence of MYR1 is necessary for processing in parasites.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis data.

claims.claim: ASP5 cleaves the TEXEL motif of MYR1.
claims.source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that ASP5 cleaves the TEXEL motif of MYR1, and that the TEXEL can function in a novel location near the C-terminus of the protein, in contrast to Plasmodium spp. where all known PEXEL sequences are located ~15–30 amino acids from the SP cleavage site (Sargeant et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on in vitro and in vivo cleavage data.

claims.claim: The TEXEL can function in a novel location near the C-terminus of the protein, in contrast to Plasmodium PEXEL sequences.
claims.source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that ASP5 cleaves the TEXEL motif of MYR1, and that the TEXEL can function in a novel location near the C-terminus of the protein, in contrast to Plasmodium spp. where all known PEXEL sequences are located ~15–30 amino acids from the SP cleavage site (Sargeant et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the location of the TEXEL in MYR1 compared to known PEXEL locations.

claims.claim: The percentage of the PVM associated with host mitochondria is reduced by 4.3-fold in Δasp5 parasites compared to wild-type.
claims.source: Quantification of HMA by TEM showed that the percentage of the PVM associated with host mitochondria was reduced by 4.3-fold in Δasp5 parasites (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative TEM data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Δasp5CRISPR parasites exhibit reduced host mitochondrial association compared to wild-type parasites.
claims.source: In contrast, Δasp5CRISPR  parasites exhibited reduced HMA, and MAF1 was incorrectly localized, appearing predominantly in punctate structures rather than at the PVM (Figure 7C, panels 2–4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 parasites exhibit correct trafficking of MAF1 and recruitment of host mitochondria to the PVM.

results.result: GRA16 contains a PEXEL-like motif (RRLAE, termed TEXEL) that is required for proteolytic processing and efficient export to the host cell nucleus. Mutation of this motif prevents processing, reduces protein stability, and blocks export.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 provide converging evidence from sequence analysis, Western blotting showing loss of processing in the AAAAE mutant, and immunofluorescence demonstrating export defects. The data directly support that the TEXEL motif is necessary for GRA16 processing and trafficking. C8 is a nomenclature decision appropriately based on functional characterization.

results.result: ASP5 is identified as the *Toxoplasma* ortholog of Plasmodium PMV based on sequence homology (33% similarity, 14% identity) and shared structural features, though with notable differences including a longer signal peptide and absence of the helix-turn-helix motif.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C13 are supported by BLAST searches, sequence alignments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and comparison with published PMV structures. The identification is appropriately conservative, noting both similarities and differences between the two proteases.

results.result: ASP5 is present as two major species (~90 and ~55 kDa) and localizes to the Golgi. The catalytic mutant ASP5MUT predominantly shows the ~90 kDa form, suggesting auto-activation produces the ~55 kDa species.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 2A) and immunofluorescence co-localization with the Golgi marker GalNAc-YFP (Figure 2B). The inference about auto-activation (C15) is reasonable based on the loss of the smaller species in the catalytic mutant, though direct evidence of auto-cleavage is not provided.

results.result: ASP5 specifically cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL peptide after the leucine residue with Km ~48 μM, optimal activity at pH 5.5, and is potently inhibited by the TEXEL-mimetic compound WEHI-586 (IC50 63 nM). Activity requires the catalytic residues and the RRL motif.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C26 are comprehensively supported by fluorogenic peptide cleavage assays (Figure 2C), LC-MS/MS identification of the cleavage site (Figure 2D), kinetic measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), pH optimization, and inhibitor studies (Figure 2F). The controls with catalytic mutant and motif mutations strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: ASP5 and PMV have overlapping but distinct substrate specificities. Both cleave RxL-containing sequences, but ASP5 requires arginine at P2 (not tolerated well by PMV) and does not efficiently cleave the KAHRP PEXEL peptide that PMV processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 are supported by comparative peptide cleavage assays (Figure 3A) showing differential processing of GRA16 TEXEL vs. KAHRP PEXEL peptides by the two enzymes. The P2 substitution experiment (C31) directly demonstrates the importance of arginine at this position for ASP5.

results.result: ASP5 has strict substrate specificity requiring arginine at P3 and P2, and leucine at P1 (RRL consensus), while residues at P1' and P2' are dispensable but influence cleavage efficiency. ASP5 processes GRA19 TEXEL (RRLSD) but not the GRA21 RELLD sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 are supported by systematic mutagenesis of the TEXEL motif (Figure 3B, 3C) showing loss of activity with conservative and non-conservative substitutions at P1-P3, and enhanced activity with P2' E>A mutation. The inference about GRA21 processing at RRLAE (C38) is reasonable given sequence identity with GRA16.

results.result: Structural modeling of ASP5 with GRA16 TEXEL reveals molecular basis for substrate specificity: the P3 arginine interacts with E506/Q549, P1 leucine is surrounded by hydrophobic residues, and P2 arginine forms additional hydrogen bonds accounting for ~50% of binding energy difference vs. threonine.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 are supported by homology modeling using PMV crystal structures and AutoDock calculations (Figure 3E). The model provides structural explanations consistent with experimental specificity data. However, C48 notes a discrepancy between modeling (predicting reduced binding with P2' E>A) and experimental data (showing enhanced activity), indicating model limitations.

results.result: Deletion of ASP5 causes a growth defect in plaque assays that is complemented by re-introduction of ASP5. The defect is not due to impaired intracellular replication at 16 hours post-infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by successful gene disruption (confirmed by PCR/sequencing, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), plaque assays showing smaller plaques (Figure 4A), complementation restoring growth, and replication assays showing no difference at 16 hr (Figure 4B). The inference that the plaque defect is not due to replication (C53) is reasonable but limited to the single timepoint tested.

results.result: In Δasp5 parasites, GRA16-HA is not processed correctly and fails to export to the host cell nucleus, instead accumulating in Golgi-like structures and the PV space, confirming ASP5 is essential for GRA16 trafficking.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are strongly supported by Western blot showing loss of processing (Figure 4C) and immunofluorescence showing mislocalization (Figure 4D) in Δasp5 parasites, mirroring the TEXEL mutant phenotype. This provides direct in vivo validation of ASP5's role.

results.result: ASP5 is required for Toxoplasma-induced up-regulation of host c-Myc. Δasp5-infected cells show 6.4-fold reduced c-Myc expression compared to wild-type infection, suggesting ASP5-dependent proteins control this phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 5B) and Western blot (Figure 5C) showing dramatic reduction in c-Myc in Δasp5-infected cells. C57-C58 appropriately cite prior work. The inference that ASP5-dependent proteins mediate this effect (C61) is reasonable but indirect.

results.result: MYR1 contains a TEXEL motif (RRLSE) located ~230 residues from the C-terminus that is cleaved by ASP5. This demonstrates the TEXEL can function at novel locations beyond the N-terminus, unlike Plasmodium PEXEL sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C71 are supported by Western blot showing loss of MYR1 processing in Δasp5 (Figure 6A), in vitro cleavage of MYR1 TEXEL peptides by ASP5 (Figure 6B), and mutagenesis showing RRLSE is necessary for processing in vivo (Figure 6D). The comparison with Plasmodium PEXEL location (C71) is appropriately cited and represents an important mechanistic difference.

results.result: ASP5 is required for efficient recruitment of host mitochondria to the PVM (4.3-fold reduction in Δasp5). MAF1 is mislocalized in Δasp5 parasites but not processed differently, suggesting ASP5 acts on other proteins that interact with MAF1.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 are supported by quantitative TEM (Figure 7B), immunofluorescence showing MAF1 mislocalization (Figure 7C), and Western blot showing no change in MAF1 processing (Figure 7D). The inference that ASP5 acts on MAF1-interacting proteins (C76) is reasonable. However, the authors note this phenotype is variable between labs, suggesting potential context-dependence.

results.result: The nanotubular network is vastly diminished and disorganized in Δasp5 vacuoles, suggesting one or more components of this network require ASP5 processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by TEM showing dramatic NTN defects in all Δasp5 vacuoles examined (Figure 7E). The inference about ASP5-dependent NTN components (C78) is reasonable but indirect, as the specific substrates are not identified.

results.result: GRA24 export is completely blocked in Δasp5 parasites and restored by complementation, but GRA24 is not directly processed by ASP5 and lacks a canonical TEXEL, indicating indirect dependence on ASP5.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are supported by immunofluorescence showing export block (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), Western blot showing no size change (Figure 8B), and peptide cleavage assays showing ASP5 does not cleave GRA24 sequences (Figure 8C). The conclusion of indirect dependence (C83) is well-reasoned based on the evidence.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis reveals that ASP5 influences the magnitude of transcriptional changes during infection. Wild-type infection significantly alters 6,771 genes (3,402 up, 3,369 down), while Δasp5 infection affects only 1,850 genes, with log-fold changes averaging 60% of wild-type levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 are supported by comprehensive RNA-seq analysis with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR 5%) and multiple replicates. The data show dramatic reduction in both number and magnitude of transcriptional changes in Δasp5 infection (Figure 9A). The inference that most genes respond partly through ASP5-dependent pathways (C89) is reasonable.

results.result: Gene Ontology analysis reveals ASP5 controls up-regulation of genes involved in cell cycle, nucleic acid metabolism, and chromatin binding, and down-regulation of genes involved in autophagy, peroxisome fission, vacuole organization, and protein trafficking.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 are supported by GO analysis of differentially expressed genes (Table 1) with appropriate statistical testing. The inference about facilitating parasite persistence (C92) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: The transcriptional profile of Δgra16 infection strongly correlates with Δasp5 infection (ROAST P=5×10⁻⁵), indicating GRA16-induced changes represent a subset of all ASP5-influenced genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are supported by gene set enrichment analysis comparing the current data with published Δgra16 data, with appropriate statistical testing (Figure 9C). This validates that GRA16 is one of multiple ASP5-dependent effectors.

results.result: ASP5 is essential for virulence in mice. Infection with 15 Δasp5 parasites is non-lethal and provides protective immunity, while 50 Δasp5 parasites show delayed mortality. Wild-type and complemented parasites are uniformly lethal at both doses.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C103 are supported by survival studies with appropriate controls including complemented parasites (Figure 10A-C). Seroconversion confirms infection occurred. The dose-response (15 vs. 50 parasites) and re-challenge experiments strengthen the conclusions. Statistical analysis is appropriate (Log-rank test).

results.result: This work identifies ASP5 as the first component of the dense granule export machinery in Toxoplasma, demonstrating its control of nanotubular network formation, mitochondrial recruitment, transcriptional changes affecting thousands of genes, and virulence in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 are summary statements appropriately supported by the collective evidence from the manuscript. These represent the major conclusions integrating multiple lines of evidence from biochemistry, cell biology, transcriptomics, and in vivo studies.
